relationship.direction: natural-regeneration potential is mapped within a 5 km radius of forest cover; beyond it the seed-source effect on regeneration is treated as negligible
only forest fragments at or above the minimum size are counted as seed sources when generating regeneration potential
natural regeneration is screened out beyond 5 km from existing natural forest — seed-source paucity and low seed-dispersal likelihood make it unlikely to occur

below 10 persons/km2 the landscape supports WIDE-SCALE restoration (single intervention type, incl. assisted or spontaneous natural regeneration and mixed-species plantations); at 10-100 persons/km2 only MOSAIC restoration applies, spatially mixed with agricultural land uses
the opportunity space for forest regrowth is land BELOW 25% tree cover that lies where forests historically occurred; restoration is the transition across that 25% threshold
regrowth is MORE likely far from roads — inaccessibility reduces clearing and browsing pressure, so for passive regeneration road distance acts opposite to its usual implementation-cost direction
regrowth likelihood increases on steep, less-accessible slopes — steepness is a positive correlate for passive regeneration because it depresses competing land use, not a biophysical optimum
regrowth likelihood increases near rivers or existing forest fragments — proximity to a seed source is a positive correlate of passive regeneration

external ecological memory: remnant forest patches or riparian vegetation within 100 m, and large forest remnants or reserves within 200 m, indicate capacity for natural regeneration — these are landscape-scale seed-source proximity indicators

where cleared land must be kept 'clean', natural regeneration can proceed only if the land is legally abandoned and tenure and property ownership relinquished — tenure arrangements can foreclose passive restoration entirely
seed availability enters the post-fire regeneration model as a kernel surface with a 150 m neighbourhood — the spatial scale at which surviving seed sources drive the odds of conifer regeneration
north- and east-facing aspects raise the odds of post-fire conifer regeneration (cooler, moister microclimate); aspect explained 14% of the variation

natural-regeneration potential is concentrated close to forest: 98.1% of sampled 30 m cells with potential >0.5 fall within 300 m of a forest edge, and potential declines with distance to existing forest
distance to forest patches is negatively associated with natural-regeneration potential — seedling density and species richness both fall as distance from the forest edge increases
natural-regeneration potential is higher where ROAD DENSITY IS LOW, because agricultural land there is more likely to be abandoned — the opposite sign to road access as an implementation-cost factor

humid tropical forests are poorly adapted to fire and are less likely to regenerate naturally after a fire event, although some recently burned areas regenerate faster under favourable conditions — burned area enters as a negative covariate

natural-regeneration potential RISES with local forest density within a 1 km radius and falls with distance to existing forest — surrounding forest is the seed and disperser supply, so this is the landscape's cover, not the site's

in Para, Brazil, secondary vegetation may be LEGALLY CLEARED below 10 m2/ha basal area (municipalities >50% primary forest) or below 5 m2/ha (<50%) — young regrowth under the threshold has no legal protection, so passive regeneration is at clearing risk until it crosses it
natural regeneration is not cost-free: stewards need compensating for fencing, fire protection and hunting patrols — the practice depends on a finance mechanism even though it needs no planting
